Yellowfin tuna Thunnus albacares is a highly migratory pelagic species whose early life history is characterized by rapid development at elevated temperatures. Field-collected eggs incubated at a constant temperature of 30.1 °C [T = 30.1 °C] hatch in approximately 1.43 days [ab = approximately 1.43 days], a remarkably short embryonic duration that reflects the warm equatorial waters where spawning typically occurs. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva measures only a few millimeters and has a wet weight of roughly 0.000463 grams [Wwb = roughly 0.000463 grams], an incredibly small initial mass that underscores the extreme fecundity required to offset massive early-life mortality. These minute prolarvae rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the lecithotrophic phase, and the rapid progression from fertilized egg to actively feeding larva is critical for survival in the oligotrophic pelagic environment.

Reproductive output in this species is among the highest recorded for any teleost, driven by the need to compensate for the negligible size and vulnerability of the offspring. Under average thermal conditions in the tropical Pacific, approximately 20 °C [T = 20 °C], a single mature female is capable of producing roughly 83,000 eggs each day [Ri = roughly 83,000 eggs each day] during the peak spawning season, with this prodigious fecundity enabling the population to sustain itself despite intense larval predation. The maximum daily reproductive output at 20 °C is truly extraordinary, as the species repeats this spawning effort over many days throughout the protracted breeding period. This strategy of producing vast numbers of small, pelagic eggs is a classic example of an r-selected life history approach that is typical of large, highly fecund scombrids.

The species exhibits a relatively rapid pace of life, though individuals can attain considerable size and substantial maximum longevity. When maintained at the thermal regime typical of their adult foraging grounds, 20 °C, the natural lifespan of Yellowfin tuna is estimated at approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years], though the maximum recorded longevity in the wild may extend beyond this value for the olde at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]st individuals. Over the course of this lifespan, adults undergo sustained somatic growth that eventually approaches an asymptotic size. The ultimate fork length attained by the largest individuals is 239 centimeters [Li = 239 centimeters], a measurement that places Thunnus albacares among the larger members of its genus, though it remains smaller than the Atlantic bluefin tuna. This large body size is supported by an energetic demand that requires constant foraging on schooling prey.

Sexual maturation occurs at a body size far smaller than the maximum attainable length, which is a common pattern among iteroparous fishes that continue growing well after reaching reproductive maturity. Yellowfin tuna typically reach puberty at a fork length of 103.3 centimeters [Lp = 103.3 centimeters], a size that corresponds to roughly 43 percent of their ultimate length and is generally achieved within the first two to three years of life. The length at reproductive maturity ranges between approximately 100 and 125 centimeters in most populations, but the centrally estimated value of 103.3 centimeters represents the typical size at which 50 percent of individuals are expected to be mature. The onset of vitellogenesis and spermatogenesis at this threshold body size marks the initiation of the adult breeding phase.

The ultimate wet weight reached by the largest adult Yellowfin tuna approaches 200,000 grams [Wwi = 200,000 grams], a massive body mass that reflects the prodigious feeding capacity of this apex predator. This maximum weight is attained after many years of sustained growth, with the heaviest specimens typically being the oldest individuals that have successfully avoided fishing mortality and natural predation throughout their lives. In stark contrast to this enormous adult mass, the initial wet weight at birth is merely 0.000463 grams [Wwb = 0.000463 grams], representing an astonishing increase in body mass of over eight orders of magnitude over the course of the lifespan. This extreme disparity between neonatal and adult mass underscores the intense selective pressures driving both high fecundity and rapid juvenile growth rates in this commercially important scombrid.
